coherence.reasons: Both run the same sound chain: growth without profit, negative unit economics, a weak pop-up, a runway breach, software instead. Y opens with an explicit test of the six conditions the founders' answer needs, and every later section maps back to one of them, ending in an options table, risks, triggers and decisions. X's summary also maps to its sections, but the same section title ('The market grows, but no one profits') is repeated on every divider, including the recommendation section. One appendix divider is also mistitled, and the argument is spread over many more slides with some repetition. Y's hierarchy is tighter and its slide titles carry the argument on their own.

judgment.reasons: Both reach the key's preferred recommendation: do not launch, grow software, sell store-based fast delivery, with re-entry triggers. Y weighs alternatives better. It builds and rejects a one-store pilot with numbers (runway breached in month 10, little new learning), which is the 'launch in one city' trap in the key. It also gives a minimum growth rate for the software path (34%), phases hires in tranches against signed contracts, sets a 90-day checkpoint and says not to extend the pop-up. X adds a useful point that an own service would turn pipeline grocers into rivals, and it has a risk table with owners. But X considers no intermediate test option, and its software stress test is thinner (60% against 30% only). Y's re-entry trigger also includes a fee-based route, reflecting the Zipcart evidence.

evidence.reasons: Both get the core figures right: −$6.17 at the median, −$1.76 on best inputs, −$12.57 for the pop-up, $2.5M and about six months of runway, and −$1.05 for the Zipcart moves on a median store. Y adds the explicit 41.5% CAGR, the break-even order value at best observed density (about $50, matching the key), and the 1,042 orders a day needed with Zipcart's moves. It also checks that the plan implies $266M of sales, more than QuickBasket's whole revenue, and builds a monthly cash model with a growth threshold. X adds the −$0.48 no-volume-loss case, a rider-pay sensitivity, a break-even rider productivity and a $13.7M acquisition estimate; the last is assumption-heavy but flagged. X never states the CAGR and gives no break-even at best density. Small errors on both sides: Y's one-driver sensitivity chart mislabels three bars (the title's conclusion is still right), and 'lose money on every order' slightly overstates the incumbents. X's 'about $0.30' understates the order-value case (−$0.73). On balance Y uses the critical evidence a little more fully.

revision.reasons: Both reject the founders' hypothesis on the evidence, as the key expects, while granting that the growth is real. Y handles it more explicitly and more fairly. It states the hypothesis, lists the six conditions it needs and tests each. It gives the pop-up a 'fair caveat' for being early, then shows that ramp-up alone does not close the gap. On Zipcart it concedes that 'a profitable route may exist, but only at top-quartile density with premium pricing', and puts a number on the density required. That is close to the key's nuanced reading. X also works through the Zipcart case (−$1.05 and −$0.48) and credits the founders on growth. But it frames Zipcart mainly as 'a price rise, not better operations' and does not say what density would make the fee route work. Its re-entry tests leave out the fee route.

overall.reasons: Both are strong, numerically sound documents that reach the defensible conclusion and avoid the main traps. Y would serve the board better. It tests the founders' hypothesis condition by condition and rejects the tempting one-store pilot with numbers. It shows what it would take for the Zipcart route to work, and it stress-tests its own software recommendation down to a 34% growth floor with phased hires and a 90-day checkpoint. It does this in a tighter structure. X is thorough and has some good extras (the channel-conflict point, the acquisition bill, the rider-pay sensitivity), but it is longer and more repetitive, omits an intermediate test option, and is less precise about when the economics could work.
